vignette:
He is a 57-year-old North American man who has spent most of his adult life making spaces feel calm, balanced, and intentional. As an interior designer, he is used to measuring light, arranging color, and thinking carefully about how people move through a room. Before the accident, he describes himself as someone who could always “see the shape of a place” and imagine how to make it work. He had been divorced for several years and lived alone, with his work providing both structure and a sense of identity.

The accident happens on an ordinary day, which is part of what makes it so difficult for him to make sense of afterward. He is driving to meet a client when another vehicle crosses into his lane and strikes him hard enough to send his car spinning. In the instant before impact, he remembers a sharp, almost crystalline awareness that he is about to die. In the months that follow, that moment becomes the one his mind returns to most often. He describes it not as a memory that he thinks about, but as something that keeps happening to him. The sound of metal, the violent jolt, and the feeling of being trapped in the wreckage recur in flashes so vivid that his body reacts as if the crash is happening again.

After the accident, he is physically injured and shaken, but it is the internal aftermath that surprises him most. He expects to recover once his body heals. Instead, he finds that he is constantly scanning for danger. When he drives, his shoulders tighten and his hands grip the wheel so hard that his knuckles whiten. He checks mirrors repeatedly, watches intersections with unusual intensity, and avoids routes that remind him of the crash. If a car comes too close, he is flooded with panic and a surge of heat in his chest, as though the collision is imminent again. He used to enjoy driving to job sites because it gave him time to think; now he plans his day around minimizing time on the road.

At home, he becomes more guarded and easily startled. Sudden noises—a door slamming, a pan dropping in the kitchen, a siren passing outside—make him jump before he can catch himself. He notices that his sleep is light and broken. Some nights he wakes abruptly from dreams of twisting metal and shattered glass, his heart racing and his sheets damp with sweat. Other nights he lies awake replaying the accident in his mind, searching for the moment he might have done something differently. The questions circle without resolving: Should he have left earlier? Taken another street? Trusted his instincts and slowed down sooner? He knows intellectually that the other driver was at fault, but emotionally he keeps returning to the idea that he should have prevented it.

His work, once a source of pleasure, becomes more complicated. He still sketches room layouts and selects fabrics, but he notices that concentration takes more effort. He can stand in a showroom and suddenly lose track of what he is looking at, his attention pulled back to the crash or to the sensation of being trapped. He is especially unsettled by anything that feels enclosed—tight hallways, crowded furniture arrangements, heavy doors that close with a sound like impact. Because his profession depends on visualizing how spaces feel, he is frustrated by the way his body now reacts before his mind can intervene. He continues to work, but he does so with a sense that part of him is always braced.

Emotionally, he has become more isolated. His divorce had already left him somewhat accustomed to solitude, but now he keeps people at a distance in a different way. He declines invitations more often, says he is tired, and avoids describing what he is going through. He is not comfortable appearing vulnerable, and he feels embarrassed by how easily he is unsettled. At times he seems flat and withdrawn, though he also has moments of irritability that catch him off guard. Small frustrations can feel disproportionate, and afterward he feels ashamed. He misses the version of himself who felt composed and competent, someone who could move through the world with confidence. Now he feels as though the accident has changed his relationship to safety itself. Even in familiar places, he is aware of exits, traffic sounds, and the possibility that something sudden could happen again.

Over time, he comes to recognize that the accident is not over in the way he once assumed. It is present in his body, in his sleep, in the way he drives, in the rooms he designs, and in the careful way he moves through each day.
